data.title: Erythroderma — viva
data.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 30 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erythroderma** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define erythroderma.**
- Generalised erythema and scaling involving ≥90% of body surface area (synonym: exfoliative dermatitis); a dermatological emergency because of systemic complications

**Q2. What are the causes? (common PYQ)**
- Pre-existing dermatoses (~50–60%): psoriasis (commonest in India), eczemas (atopic, airborne contact — parthenium, seborrhoeic, chronic actinic dermatitis), pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen planus, pemphigus foliaceus, ichthyoses, crusted scabies, dermatophytosis
- Drugs (~15–20%): antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone), allopurinol, sulphonamides, dapsone, β-lactams, anti-TB drugs, gold, NSAIDs, also topical medicaments
- Malignancy (~10%): cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary syndrome, erythrodermic MF), leukaemia, Hodgkin's, paraneoplastic (solid tumours)
- Idiopathic (~10–30%) — 'red man syndrome' in elderly men; some later declare CTCL
- Neonates/infants: ichthyoses (CIE, Netherton), SSSS, immunodeficiency (Omenn), seborrhoeic dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis

**Q3. Clues to the underlying cause on examination.**
- Psoriasis: silvery scales on scalp, nail pits/oil-drop, history; may lose typical features
- PRP: islands of sparing, orange-red waxy palmoplantar keratoderma, follicular papules on knuckles
- Atopic/eczema: lichenification, intense itch, raised IgE
- Airborne contact: worse on exposed sites, seasonal flares
- Drug: recent drug, morbilliform onset, fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy (DRESS)
- CTCL: intense itch, lymphadenopathy, leonine facies, palmoplantar keratoderma, ectropion, alopecia, nail dystrophy, circulating Sézary cells
- Pemphigus foliaceus: crusted erosions, cornflake scales, Nikolsky positive
- Crusted scabies: hyperkeratosis on hands, nails, contacts itching

**Q4. Describe the clinical features.**
- Onset acute (drugs, eczema) or insidious (CTCL, idiopathic); redness then scaling (fine bran-like in eczema, large sheets in drug), pruritus, oedema, lichenification
- Hair: telogen effluvium/alopecia; nails: Beau's lines, shiny nails, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis; ectropion, epiphora
- Systemic: chills (loss of thermoregulation), lymphadenopathy (dermatopathic), hepatomegaly, pedal oedema, tachycardia
- Palmoplantar keratoderma — PRP, CTCL, psoriasis

**Q5. Describe the pathophysiological consequences / complications.**
- Thermoregulation failure — hypothermia or hyperthermia
- Increased transepidermal water loss → dehydration, electrolyte imbalance; loss of protein in scales (up to 20–30 g/day) → hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, negative nitrogen balance
- Increased cutaneous blood flow → high-output cardiac failure in elderly
- Secondary infection (S. aureus), sepsis, pneumonia
- Gynaecomastia, anaemia (iron, folate loss), dermatopathic lymphadenopathy
- Dermatogenic enteropathy (malabsorption) — PYQ

**Q6. What is dermatogenic enteropathy? (PYQ)**
- Reversible malabsorption (steatorrhoea, reduced D-xylose absorption) and protein-losing enteropathy in patients with extensive skin disease like erythroderma/psoriasis; improves when skin improves

**Q7. How do you investigate erythroderma?**
- CBC (eosinophilia — drug, atopic, CTCL; anaemia), ESR, total protein/albumin, electrolytes, renal and liver function, blood sugar
- Peripheral smear for Sézary cells; flow cytometry (CD4:CD8 >10, CD7/CD26 loss), TCR gene rearrangement
- Multiple skin biopsies (repeat if non-diagnostic — 50% give the cause), lymph node biopsy if suspicious
- KOH and skin scraping for scabies/tinea; IgE; DIF if pemphigus foliaceus suspected
- Chest X-ray, ultrasound abdomen, HIV, cultures if febrile; age-appropriate malignancy screening

**Q8. Histopathology.**
- Often non-specific: hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, acanthosis, spongiosis, perivascular infiltrate
- Specific features in ~50%: psoriasis (regular acanthosis, Munro microabscesses), PRP (alternating ortho/parakeratosis — chequerboard), CTCL (epidermotropism, Pautrier microabscesses, atypical cerebriform lymphocytes), drug (eosinophils, necrotic keratinocytes), PF (subcorneal acantholysis)

**Q9. Management — general.**
- Admit severe cases; warm room, monitor temperature, fluids, input–output, weight
- Bland emollients (white soft paraffin, liquid paraffin) frequently; wet wraps; oatmeal baths; low/mid-potency topical steroids (avoid extensive potent use); sedating antihistamines
- High-protein diet, correct electrolytes, albumin; treat infection; manage cardiac failure
- Stop all non-essential drugs

**Q10. Specific treatment according to cause.**
- Psoriasis: methotrexate, cyclosporine (fast), acitretin, biologics (infliximab, IL-17/23 inhibitors); avoid systemic steroids (rebound pustular flare); avoid phototherapy in acute phase
- Eczema/airborne: systemic steroids short course, azathioprine, cyclosporine, methotrexate, dupilumab (atopic)
- Drug-induced: withdraw, steroids for DRESS
- PRP: retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin), methotrexate, biologics (IL-17, TNF)
- CTCL: refer — ECP, bexarotene, interferon, mogamulizumab, chemotherapy
- Idiopathic: symptomatic + long-term follow-up for evolving CTCL

**Q11. Prognosis.**
- Depends on cause — drug-induced resolves fastest (weeks); psoriasis/eczema relapse; idiopathic chronic; mortality 20–40% historically in elderly due to sepsis, cardiac failure; CTCL poor prognosis

**Q12. Differentiate erythroderma due to Sézary syndrome from benign causes.**
- Sézary: triad of erythroderma, generalised lymphadenopathy, circulating clonal atypical T cells (≥1000/µL Sézary cells, CD4:CD8 ≥10, loss of CD7 ≥40% or CD26 ≥30%), intense itch, keratoderma, leonine facies, alopecia; poor response to steroids

**Q13. How do you approach an erythroderma patient in the ward (step-by-step)?**
- Stabilise: vitals, temperature, hydration, urine output, sepsis screen, cardiac status
- History: prior dermatosis, drugs (last 8 weeks), atopy, photosensitivity, systemic symptoms (weight loss, nodes, itch severity), family history
- Examine for clues: scalp, nails, palms/soles, islands of sparing, mucosa, lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly
- Investigate: bloods, multiple biopsies, Sézary screen, KOH/scrapings, IgE, imaging
- Treat: supportive + cause-specific; avoid starting many new drugs

**Q14. Drug-induced erythroderma — which drugs and features?**
- Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone, allopurinol, dapsone, sulfonamides, β-lactams, vancomycin, anti-TB drugs, gold, lithium, calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs; often part of DRESS (fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, hepatitis) — RegiSCAR scoring; onset 2–8 weeks after drug; fastest resolution after withdrawal

**Q15. Describe erythrodermic psoriasis triggers and management.**
- Triggers: abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids/ potent topicals, phototherapy burn, infection, HIV, stress, lithium/antimalarials, alcohol
- Management: admit; bland emollients; cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg (rapid) or infliximab/ IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors; methotrexate or acitretin for maintenance; avoid steroids; fluids and temperature control

**Q16. What is the 'red man syndrome' (idiopathic erythroderma of elderly)?**
- Chronic idiopathic erythroderma in elderly men with marked itch, lichenification, palmoplantar keratoderma, dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, raised IgE; evolves to CTCL in some — repeated biopsies and T-cell clonality/flow cytometry every 6–12 months

**Q17. Neonatal and infantile erythroderma — causes and approach.**
- Ichthyoses (collodion baby, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, Netherton — bamboo hair, hypernatraemic dehydration), SSSS, seborrhoeic/atopic dermatitis, immunodeficiency (Omenn, SCID, Wiskott–Aldrich, hyper-IgE), diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis, metabolic (biotinidase, multiple carboxylase, zinc, essential fatty acid deficiency), maternal GVHD, psoriasis
- Investigate: hair microscopy, immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets, zinc/biotin, skin biopsy; manage dehydration, hypernatraemia, temperature, sepsis

**Q18. Why should systemic steroids be avoided in psoriatic erythroderma but may be used in others?**
- Steroid withdrawal precipitates generalised pustular psoriasis/ rebound erythroderma; in drug-induced (DRESS), eczematous/airborne contact, pemphigus foliaceus and some idiopathic cases steroids are useful with careful tapering

**Q19. Fluid and nutrition care in erythroderma.**
- Daily weight, input–output charts; extra fluids for insensible losses (≈ 2–4 l/day extra), correct electrolytes (Na, K), monitor albumin; high-protein (1.5–2 g/kg) and high-calorie diet, vitamin/ iron/ folate supplements; avoid hypothermia (warm room 30–32 °C, blankets)

**Q20. Cardiac complications and why.**
- Generalised cutaneous vasodilation increases blood flow (up to 10–20% of cardiac output) → high-output cardiac failure, tachycardia, especially in elderly with heart disease; monitor ECG, avoid fluid overload

**Q21. Lymphadenopathy in erythroderma — dermatopathic vs lymphoma.**
- Dermatopathic lymphadenitis: reactive, soft, mobile, paracortical expansion with melanin- and lipid-laden macrophages and Langerhans cells
- Lymphoma: hard, rapidly enlarging, matted; atypical cells, clonal TCR — biopsy suspicious nodes (excisional)

**Q22. Nail and hair changes in erythroderma.**
- Nails: Beau's lines, onycholysis, shiny polished nails (rubbing), subungual hyperkeratosis (psoriasis/PRP/crusted scabies), onychomadesis
- Hair: telogen effluvium, diffuse alopecia (CTCL may have alopecia with 'leonine facies'), madarosis

**Q23. Erythroderma in HIV.**
- Causes: psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, drug reactions (nevirapine, cotrimoxazole), crusted scabies, PRP type VI, CTCL, chronic actinic dermatitis; check CD4 and viral load; treat cause and optimise ART

**Q24. What is pityriasis rubra pilaris erythroderma's characteristic picture?**
- Orange-red erythroderma with sharply demarcated islands of sparing ('nappes claires'), follicular papules on knuckles, waxy orange keratoderma (sandal), fine bran-like scales; responds to retinoids/ methotrexate/ IL-17 inhibitors

**Q25. Pemphigus foliaceus erythroderma — clues.**
- Crusted, scaly, oozing erosions with 'cornflake' scales on seborrhoeic areas, positive Nikolsky, no mucosal involvement, smell; biopsy (subcorneal acantholysis), DIF intercellular IgG, anti-Dsg1 ELISA

**Q26. Crusted scabies presenting as erythroderma — clues.**
- Thick crusts over hands, feet, extensors, scalp and nails, sometimes little itch, immunocompromised/elderly/ institutionalised, outbreak among staff and contacts; mineral oil scraping shows abundant mites — isolate and treat with ivermectin + topical scabicide

**Q27. What follow-up is needed after recovery?**
- Treat underlying disease, review drugs (drug card), monitor for relapse, repeat biopsies in idiopathic cases for CTCL every 6–12 months, maintain skin care with emollients

**Q28. Describe the Sézary cell.**
- Atypical T lymphocyte with hyperchromatic convoluted ('cerebriform') nucleus, scant cytoplasm (CD4+, CD7−, CD26− typically); >1000/µl in blood (B2 blood involvement) defines Sézary syndrome with clonal TCR

**Q29. Prognosis by cause in erythroderma.**
- Best: drug-induced (resolves in weeks after withdrawal), eczema
- Intermediate: psoriasis, PRP (relapses)
- Worst: Sézary syndrome/CTCL (median survival ~2–5 years), idiopathic in elderly (chronic, may evolve)

**Q30. Exfoliative dermatitis in children due to SSSS — management.**
- Admit, IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (cloxacillin/ cefazolin; clindamycin to reduce toxin), fluids, temperature control, gentle skin care with emollients, analgesia; no steroids; heals without scarring in 1–2 weeks

## Quick spotter facts
- ≥90% BSA red and scaly — erythroderma
- Islands of sparing + orange keratoderma — PRP
- Erythroderma + nodes + Sézary cells — Sézary syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Erythroderma). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
